claims: The Pharisees were an influential Jewish social movement and school of thought in Palestine during the Second Temple period (c. 515 BCE–70 CE).
The Pharisees adhered strictly to both written law and oral tradition.
The Pharisees emphasized personal piety and ritual purity.
The Pharisees believed in the resurrection of the dead, afterlife, and the existence of angels.
The Pharisees believed in the binding force of oral tradition, or the "unwritten Torah," alongside the written Mosaic law.
The Pharisees believed in divine providence combined with human free will.
The Pharisees believed in the immortality of the soul.
The Pharisees were often middle-class.
The Pharisees were popular with the common people.
The Pharisees served as leaders in synagogues.
The strict school of Shammai and the more lenient school of Hillel.
The Pharisees meticulously applied Levitical purity laws, originally meant for priests, to daily life and meals.
According to JewishEncyclopedia.com, the Pharisees were scrupulous about paying tithes and offering.
The Pharisees emphasized study and interpretation of the law.
The Pharisees shifted focus away from exclusive reliance on Temple sacrifices.
The Temple was destroyed in 70 AD.
After the Temple's destruction in 70 AD, Pharisaic beliefs became the foundation of Rabbinic Judaism.
In the New Testament, the Pharisees are often portrayed as opponents of Jesus due to their legalism and public hypocrisy.
Nicodemus was sympathetic to Jesus.
The Apostle Paul was an early follower of Jesus.
The Sadducees were aristocratic.
The Sadducees only accepted the written Torah.
The Gospels often show conflict between the Pharisees and Jesus over ritual minutiae, such as fasting and Sabbath.
In the Gospels, the Pharisees prioritized outward observance over internal righteousness.
